title: Institutional Construction AI: How Canadian GCs Review Drawings and Specs Before Bid Day
summary: Canadian institutional GCs face the most complex document sets. See how AI reviews drawings and specs together to catch scope gaps before bid day.

## TL;DR


- Institutional projects in Canada carry the most complex document sets in ICI construction: hospitals, post-secondary facilities, and courthouses routinely run to tens of thousands of pages.
- Scope gaps on institutional work are rarely random. They follow predictable patterns in MEP, envelope, and specialty trades.
- The Dodge Momentum Index shows institutional planning up 4.9% in August 2026. More pursuits are coming, and pre-construction teams need faster, more reliable document review.
- AI tools built for GC pre-construction now read the full project set together: drawings, specs, and addenda in one pass, not one file at a time.
- Provision's[Scope Agent](https://provision.com/scope-agent) and[Risk Review](https://provision.com/risk-review) are built for exactly this workflow. Every finding is source-traced to the exact page and section.


Institutional construction is where document complexity becomes a liability. A hospital tower or a post-secondary campus project can land on your desk with 1,500 drawing sheets, six addenda, and a specification manual that runs past 2,000 pages. Your pre-construction team has two weeks to price it, write scope packages for 40 trades, and flag every gap before bid day.


That is not a document review problem. It is a risk management problem.


The Dodge Momentum Index reported a 4.9% increase in institutional planning starts in August 2026. That signal matters for Canadian GCs competing in the ICI sector. More hospitals, more post-secondary facilities, more courthouses. Each one more complex than the last.


This article covers how Canadian institutional GCs are using AI to review drawings and specs together, what that changes for bid-day accuracy, and where the gaps most often hide.


## Why Institutional Document Sets Are Different


Commercial construction is complex. Institutional construction is a different category entirely.


A hospital imaging suite adds lead-lined walls, shielding specs, and specialized MEP requirements that do not appear in a standard commercial project. A post-secondary science building adds fume hoods, gas piping, and biosafety exhaust systems. A courthouse adds security infrastructure, ballistic-rated glazing, and holding cell requirements.


Each adds drawing layers, spec sections, and trade interfaces that your scope packages need to reflect accurately. Miss one and you either carry it yourself or fight a change order at construction.


One example from Provision's[Scope Gap Playbook](https://provision.com/ebooks/scope-gap-playbook) : a GC absorbed a $300,000 scope gap on lead-lined glass in a hospital imaging suite. The drawings called for it. The specs described it. Nobody's scope said who supplied it. The GC carried the cost under "readily inferable" contract language.


That is not an edge case. It is the pattern.


## The Document Review Problem Canadian GCs Face in 2026


Most pre-construction teams still review documents the same way they did ten years ago. One estimator opens the drawings. Another reads the specs. A third checks addenda. Each works from their own file.


The problem is that institutional scope gaps almost never live in one document. They live in the space between documents.


The architectural drawings show the roof assembly. The spec describes the cover board. The structural drawings add a loading condition. None of the three explicitly assigns the cover board to a trade. Your roofing scope does not include it. Your general trades scope does not include it. The gap costs $400,000 on a $50 million project, as documented in the Scope Gap Playbook.


Reading documents one file at a time makes cross-document gaps invisible. You need a review process that holds the entire project set at once.


### How Many Pages Are Actually in an Institutional Bid Package?


Provision's[Chat Agent](https://provision.com/chat-agent) can read up to 100,000 pages per project. That ceiling exists for a reason. Institutional project document sets routinely push into five-figure page counts when you count drawing sheets, specification sections, geotechnical reports, environmental studies, and addenda together.


A single addendum on a hospital project can modify 200 drawing sheets and add three new specification sections. A manual review catches some of it. It does not catch all of it. And the items it misses are the ones that become change orders.


## What AI Document Review Actually Does on an Institutional Bid


The word "AI" is overused in construction software marketing. Here is what it means in practice for a pre-construction team reviewing an institutional bid package.


### It Reviews the Full Document Set, Not One File at a Time


Provision's Scope Agent ingests drawings, specifications, tables, and notes together. It does not read the architectural drawings in isolation from the structural or MEP drawings. It reads the full set and flags where the documents conflict or leave work unassigned.


When an addendum arrives, the tool handles it automatically. You do not restart the review. The addendum is incorporated and the scope packages update to reflect the change.


### It Generates Trade-Specific Scope Packages with Source Citations


Scope Agent generates coordinated scope packages by trade. Each item in the scope package is traced back to the exact drawing sheet and specification section that requires it.


Your estimator does not have to trust that the AI found the right item. They can verify it. Every scope item has a page reference. That is the standard on institutional work, where owners and their consultants will challenge any scope assumption without documentation.


On Provision's internal validation dataset, Scope Agent achieved 97.01% match accuracy on scope item extraction. The human estimator baseline on the same exercise was 91.3%, at roughly four days per project.


### It Surfaces Coordination Gaps Between Trades


Provision's[Scope Gap Index](https://provision.com/scope-gap-index) , covering 1,290 scope packages across 24 projects from 16 general contractors in Q3 2026, found that 74% of packages had at least one coordination flag. That means work sitting between two trades, with neither scope naming it.


Those flags are model-generated and mark potential gaps that an estimator still needs to verify. On institutional projects, they cluster in predictable places:


- **Anchors, embeds, and connections:** flagged in 48% of all 1,290 packages reviewed. The steel sub needs an embed cast into the concrete sub's slab. Neither scope names who supplies it.
- **Sealants, flashing, and waterproofing joints:** flagged in 45% of packages. The roofer stops and the cladding sub starts. The joint between them belongs to nobody.
- **Penetrations, sleeves, and firestopping:** flagged in 39% of packages. The pipe goes through the rated wall. Nobody's scope says who sleeves it, who seals it, and who signs for the inspection.
- **Testing, inspection, and certification:** flagged in 47% of Division 01 packages. The spec requires the test. No scope says who pays for it.


These are not edge cases on institutional work. They are the standard pattern. The Scope Gap Index tells you which gaps to look for before the bid leaves your office.


## MEP and Specialty Trade Gaps on Institutional Projects


MEP scope gaps on institutional projects carry more financial exposure than on commercial work. The systems are more complex, the inspections are more rigorous, and the owner's consultants are more likely to enforce "readily inferable" contract language.


The[Scope Gap Playbook's trade-specific chapter](https://provision.com/ebooks/scope-gap-playbook/trade-specific-scope-gaps) documents the recurring gaps by trade. For institutional work, the ones that cost the most include:


- **Generator field conditioning:** the spec requires it, the drawings show the generator location, and no scope says who conditions the installation environment. Costs recur across projects at the "millions" level according to operators interviewed for the playbook.
- **Fire-rated louvres:** the MEP drawings show the opening. The architectural drawings call for the rating. The scope packages split between mechanical and architectural with neither claiming the louvre.
- **Motor starters:** specified in the electrical drawings, priced by nobody, flagged as a change order after the building is roughed in.
- **Lead-lined glass:** as noted above, a $300,000 gap on a hospital imaging suite, absorbed by the GC under readily inferable language.
- **Elevator and specialty equipment testing and certification:** Division 14 packages in the Scope Gap Index had a 95% flag rate, with testing and certification as the most common issue in 73% of those packages.


An estimator who has priced 20 hospitals knows to look for these. An estimator pricing their second institutional project does not. AI document review systematizes what your most experienced estimators know, and it applies it consistently across every pursuit.


## Contract Risk on Institutional Work: Readily Inferable Language


Canadian institutional owners use standard CCDC contract forms. They also add supplementary conditions that expand the GC's scope obligations. The phrase "readily inferable" appears in those conditions and it is expensive.


When an item is "readily inferable" from the contract documents, the GC is expected to include it even if no drawing, spec, or schedule explicitly assigns it. Owners and their consultants use this language aggressively on institutional projects because the consultant teams are large, the document coordination is imperfect, and the gaps are real.


Provision's[Risk Review](https://provision.com/risk-review) catches this exposure before bid day. It reviews contracts, supplementary conditions, and specifications together. It flags the clauses that shift risk to the GC, compares them against default positions, and generates a risk register with severity levels (high, medium, low) and citations to the exact clause.


On Provision's platform, Risk Review has achieved 99% accuracy on risk identification. The 80% reduction in review time means your pre-construction team can review a full CCDC package, including supplementary conditions, in a fraction of the time a manual review takes.


As one Estimating Manager at a Canadian ICI GC put it in Provision's research: "If you miss anything, they'll bill it." That is the operating reality on institutional work.


## How the Pre-Bid Walk Changes When Your Document Review Is Already Done


The[Scope Gap Playbook](https://provision.com/ebooks/scope-gap-playbook) identifies eight habits that separate high-margin pre-construction teams from the rest. Habit 5 is: the pre-bid walk is a scoping tool, not a courtesy.


When your document review is complete before the walk, the walk becomes a verification exercise. Your estimator arrives with a list of flagged items. They are looking to confirm whether the drawings reflect what is actually on site. They are not trying to absorb the project for the first time while walking through it.


That changes the quality of your questions at the pre-bid meeting. It changes the quality of your scope packages. And it changes your exposure on bid day.

## The Accuracy Question: What Does 97% Mean on a Real Bid?


When a VP of Pre-Construction sees an accuracy number, the first question is: accurate compared to what?


Scope Agent's 97.01% match accuracy was measured on Provision's internal validation dataset against human-prepared scope sheets. The human estimator baseline on the same dataset was 91.3%. That is a 5.7 percentage-point gap, measured on the same drawings, same specifications, same scope items.


Every scope item Scope Agent surfaces is traced to its source: the exact drawing sheet or specification section that requires it. Your estimator reviews the output and verifies the citation. That traceability is what separates a tool you can trust from one you have to second-guess.
